newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan concerned over health of Social Security.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan concerned over health of Social Security.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Tuesday voiced considerable concern about the long-term health of the Social Security system and questioned whether modest changes would be enough to fix it.

He also made clear that he did not think that simply investing some of the Social Security funds in the stock market, rather than in U.S. Treasury bonds, would be enough to solve the system's problems.
"I think we ought to have considerable concerns (about the future health of Social Security)," he told the Senate Budget Committee. "The reasons are demographic," he added.
On its face, the system's future financing problems could be resolved by a 2.2 percentage point increase in payroll taxes.

But Greenspan voiced some scepticism about such a "simple fix" because of the possibility that Social Security may go bankrupt earlier than now envisaged. The system is now widely exepcted to into the red in the year 2029.
"History shows we tend to over-estimate the soundness of the system," Greenspan said.
However, he made clear that he did not think that merely shifting Social Security funds from lower-yielding bonds into higher-yielding stocks was the answer to the system's woes.
Asked if he was worried about the market impact of investing Social Security funds into stocks, Greenspan replied, "I would have concerns."
Unless savings are increased at the same time, the gains made by the Social Security trust fund by investing in equities would be offset by losses at private pension funds, he said.
